name: Equal Temperament Frequency
description: Gives the frequency in hertz of a pitch a given number of semitones from A4, as 440 times 2 to the power of semitones over 12. Each semitone multiplies frequency by the twelfth root of 2 in equal temperament.
notes: The semitone count is signed: positive goes up, negative goes down from A4. It assumes A4 = 440 Hz and 12-tone equal temperament, not just intonation.

name: Interval in Cents
description: Measures a musical interval in cents from the ratio of two frequencies, as 1200 times the base-2 logarithm of the ratio. One octave is 1200 cents and one equal-tempered semitone is 100 cents.
notes: Enter the upper frequency over the lower so the result is positive; equal frequencies give 0 cents. The measure is logarithmic, so equal cents mean equal perceived interval size.

name: Frequency Ratio from Cents
description: Converts an interval size in cents into a frequency ratio, as 2 raised to the power of cents over 1200. It is the inverse of the cents formula, turning a logarithmic interval back into a multiplicative frequency factor.
notes: Result is a dimensionless ratio to multiply a base frequency by; 1200 cents gives exactly 2. Negative cents yield a ratio below 1, lowering the pitch.

name: Mersenne's Law (String Frequency)
description: Computes the fundamental frequency in hertz of a vibrating string from its length, tension, and linear mass density, as one over twice the length times the square root of tension over density. Higher tension raises pitch; greater length or mass lowers it.
notes: Use SI units: length in meters, tension in newtons, density in kg/m. It gives the fundamental only for an ideal flexible string, ignoring stiffness and overtones.

name: Open Pipe Fundamental Frequency
description: Gives the fundamental frequency in hertz of a pipe open at both ends, as the speed of sound divided by twice the pipe length. Such a pipe supports a full wavelength of twice its length at the fundamental.
notes: Applies to pipes open at both ends, which produce all harmonics. It omits the end correction, so real pipes sound slightly lower than predicted.

name: Closed Pipe Fundamental Frequency
description: Gives the fundamental frequency in hertz of a pipe closed at one end, as the speed of sound divided by four times the pipe length. A closed pipe fits a quarter wavelength, sounding an octave lower than an open pipe of equal length.
notes: Applies to pipes closed at one end, which produce only odd harmonics. It omits the end correction, so real instruments sound slightly lower.

name: Pipe Frequency with End Correction
description: Computes an open pipe's fundamental frequency in hertz including an end correction, dividing the speed of sound by twice the effective length, where the effective length adds 0.6 times the diameter. This corrects for air vibrating just beyond the open end.
notes: All lengths must be in the same unit. The 0.6d factor is an approximation for one end; wide pipes need a larger correction and the constant varies with flanging.

name: nth Harmonic Frequency
description: Gives the frequency in hertz of the nth harmonic of a tone, as the harmonic number times the fundamental frequency. The harmonics form the integer-multiple series that shapes an instrument's timbre.
notes: Here n=1 is the fundamental itself, so the nth harmonic is the (n-1)th overtone. This assumes an ideal harmonic series; real strings and pipes are slightly inharmonic.

name: Beat Period from BPM
description: Converts a tempo in beats per minute to the duration of one beat in milliseconds, as 60000 divided by the BPM. It answers how many milliseconds each beat lasts at a given tempo.
notes: Output is milliseconds because 60000 is 60 seconds in ms; use 60 instead for seconds. One beat here means one quarter note in common time.

name: Note Duration from Tempo
description: Gives the duration in milliseconds of a note of a given value at a set tempo, as 240000 divided by BPM times the note value, where 4 is a quarter note and 8 an eighth. Larger note values give shorter durations.
notes: The note value follows the fraction convention (4=quarter, 8=eighth, 16=sixteenth). Output is milliseconds and assumes the beat is a quarter note.

name: Tempo-Synced Delay Time
description: Computes a tempo-synced delay time in milliseconds, as 60000 divided by BPM times the number of subdivisions per beat. Higher subdivision counts give shorter echoes that lock to the musical grid.
notes: Subdivisions per beat set the rhythmic value: 1 is a quarter, 2 an eighth, 4 a sixteenth. Output is milliseconds; use dotted or triplet factors for those feels.

name: Speed of Sound from Temperature
description: Estimates the speed of sound in air in m/s from temperature, as 331.3 times the square root of one plus temperature in Celsius over 273.15. Sound travels faster as air warms.
notes: Temperature must be in degrees Celsius; the formula converts to absolute temperature internally. It is for dry air at standard pressure and ignores humidity effects.

name: Wavelength of a Pitch
description: Gives the wavelength in meters of a sound of a given frequency, as the speed of sound divided by frequency. Lower pitches have longer wavelengths, which matters for room modes and speaker placement.
notes: Use a speed of sound matching the actual air temperature for accuracy. Frequency in hertz and speed in m/s give wavelength in meters.

name: String Tension for Target Pitch
description: Computes the tension in newtons a string needs to sound a target pitch, as the linear mass density times the square of twice the length times the frequency. It inverts Mersenne's law to solve for the required tension.
notes: Use SI units: density in kg/m, length in meters, frequency in hertz. It gives the fundamental-mode tension for an ideal string and ignores stiffness.

name: Fret Position on a String
description: Gives the distance in meters from the nut to the nth fret, as the scale length times one minus 2 to the power of minus n over 12. Frets follow the twelfth-root-of-2 spacing of equal temperament, crowding together toward the bridge.
notes: Distance is measured from the nut, not the bridge, and shares units with scale length. It assumes ideal equal temperament and no compensation for string stiffness or intonation.

name: Phons from Sones
description: Converts loudness in sones to loudness level in phons, as 40 plus 10 times the base-2 logarithm of the sone value. Each doubling of sones adds 10 phons, reflecting that a doubling of sones is a doubling of perceived loudness.
notes: Valid above 1 sone (40 phons), where the doubling relationship holds; below that the scale bends. Phons equal decibels only at 1 kHz on equal-loudness contours.

name: Sones from Phons
description: Converts a loudness level in phons to loudness in sones, as 2 to the power of phons minus 40 over 10. It inverts the sone-phon relation so that every 10-phon rise doubles the sone value and the perceived loudness.
notes: Reference point is 1 sone at 40 phons. The formula holds above 40 phons; below that perceived loudness falls off faster than it predicts.

name: Eyring Reverberation Time
description: Estimates reverberation time RT60 in seconds using the Eyring equation, from room volume, total surface area, and the mean absorption coefficient. It predicts how long sound takes to decay by 60 dB, and stays valid in rooms with high absorption.
notes: The mean absorption coefficient is a fraction between 0 and 1; the logarithm term makes it more accurate than Sabine's formula when absorption is large. The 0.161 constant assumes SI units.

name: Critical Distance (Room Acoustics)
description: Estimates the critical distance in meters from a sound source, where the direct and reverberant sound fields are equal, as 0.057 times the square root of room volume over reverberation time. Beyond it, reverberant sound dominates.
notes: Volume is in cubic meters and RT60 in seconds; the 0.057 constant assumes an omnidirectional source in SI units. Directional sources shift the true critical distance.

name: Doppler-Shifted Pitch
description: Computes the frequency in hertz heard from a source moving toward a stationary listener, as the source frequency times the speed of sound over the speed of sound minus the source speed. Approaching motion raises the pitch.
notes: This form assumes the listener is at rest and the source moves toward them; a receding source needs a sign change on vs. Source speed must stay below the speed of sound.

name: MIDI Note Number to Frequency
description: Converts a MIDI note number to its frequency in hertz, as 440 times 2 to the power of the note number minus 69 over 12. Note 69 is A4 at 440 Hz, and each step of one adds a semitone.
notes: Assumes A4 = 440 Hz and 12-tone equal temperament; MIDI 69 is the reference. Middle C is note 60, though some software labels it C3 versus C4.

name: Frequency to MIDI Note Number
description: Converts a frequency in hertz to a MIDI note number, as 69 plus 12 times the base-2 logarithm of the frequency over 440. It inverts the MIDI-to-frequency map, returning A4 = 69 and adding 12 per octave.
notes: Result is generally non-integer; round to the nearest whole number for the closest note and read the fraction as cents of detuning. Assumes A4 = 440 Hz.

name: Sound Pressure Level Ratio (dB)
description: Gives the level difference in decibels between two sound pressures, as 20 times the base-10 logarithm of their ratio. The factor of 20 applies because sound intensity scales with pressure squared.
notes: Both pressures use the same unit since only their ratio matters; enter the reference as p1. A pressure ratio of 10 equals 20 dB, and doubling the pressure is about 6 dB.

name: Frequency After n Octaves
description: Computes the frequency reached after shifting a base frequency f0 up by a given number of octaves. Each octave doubles the pitch, so the result is f0 multiplied by 2 raised to the octave count.
notes: The octave count need not be an integer; fractional values give intermediate pitches. Use a negative count to shift down. Base frequency and result share the same unit (Hz).
